properties.decision: DECIDED 2026-07-25 by Anthony: option (c), A GRAPH PER OWNERSHIP BOUNDARY WITH LEVELS INSIDE EACH. A design is its own graph when something at that level is separately OWNED, separately RELEASED, or separately SHARED — and a subtree of one graph otherwise. The hierarchy does not decide; authority does. That is the shape federated systems engineering actually uses, and it makes the split rule non-arbitrary: you can always answer "why is this its own design?" with a name, a release train, or a recipient. WHAT FOLLOWS, and each is an obligation rather than a detail. (1) THE COORDINATE. Edges cannot cross stores because the schema validates both endpoints, so a link between designs is not an edge: the other side's published surface is MIRRORED into your graph as local nodes, and the mirror carries the coordinate — which design it came from, at what content hash, when. Your own components then PROVIDE and CONSUME the mirrored Interface with ordinary local edges, so the golden thread works unchanged and foreignness is a property of the NODE rather than of the link. Same reasoning as dec:fork-point-address: a coordinate resolved against a document, never a live ref layer. (2) ROLL-UP. A parent's view of a composed child must derive from the child's own evidence or a requirement satisfied inside the child fires unsatisfied in the parent forever — cap:derived-completion's computation one level up. (3) FRESHNESS. A mirror is a dated claim about a VERSION, so a newer surface with a different hash makes it stale and that must be detectable, never assumed current (the cap:freshness and confirmation-ledger shape). (4) THE SEAM. Two teams changing the boundary itself still collide, in the one place the merge machinery does not reach; the published-surface document is what they are actually negotiating over. THE ROADS NOT TAKEN, kept because req:roads-not-taken says they are part of the record. (a) ONE GRAPH, ZOOM BY LEVEL was not rejected — it was BUILT FIRST and remains correct for everything inside one ownership boundary; cap:scoped-analysis delivers it, and (c) is a superset rather than a replacement. What (a) alone could not do is give two owners separate write locks, separate release trains, or a way to share one part without sharing everything. (b) A GRAPH PER SYSTEM was rejected as a RULE, not as a possibility: a system that is separately owned still gets its own graph under (c), but depth alone stops being sufficient reason, because every seam costs a coordinate, a roll-up and a freshness check, and a three-level tower of graphs inside one team buys none of what those cost. THE TENSION THIS RESOLVES, and it should be resolved out loud: docs/org-scale-vision.md records the destination as "one graph the whole company plans in". Under (c) that is no longer the destination — an enterprise is many designs federated at ownership boundaries, and the CEO's objectives are one design that others mirror rather than one graph everyone writes into. That document now describes a road not taken and should say so.
properties.name: DECIDED — a graph per ownership boundary, levels inside each
properties.rationale: Raised 2026-07-25 as brainstorming, because Anthony said plainly he was not convinced by the collaboration design and an unconvinced author is a finding rather than a disagreement to be argued down. Promoted to intent the same day, and COLLAPSED the same day on his word ("let's do (c) option"). THE SEQUENCE IS THE ARGUMENT for why this was worth holding open for a few hours rather than deciding immediately: option (a)'s scope filter was built FIRST precisely because it forecloses nothing, so by the time the decision was made there was working evidence about what per-level analysis actually feels like — and (a) turned out to be a subset of (c) rather than a rival to it. Deciding on day one would have been a guess; deciding after building the cheap half was a choice with evidence behind it. WHY (c) OVER (b), stated as the discriminator that survived from the brainstorm: every seam between designs costs a coordinate, an evidence roll-up and a freshness check, so a level earns its own graph only when it is separately owned, released or shared. A three-level tower of graphs inside one team pays all of that and buys none of it. (b) is not forbidden by this — a separately-owned system still gets its own design — it is that DEPTH stops being sufficient reason. WHAT THIS COSTS, recorded so nobody is surprised: docs/org-scale-vision.md's "one graph the whole company plans in" is now a road not taken, and req:concurrent-planning's answer changes shape — ownership boundaries become the primary isolation mechanism, with the claims layer and the merge driver serving work INSIDE one boundary rather than across all of them. The first rung built on this decision is the coordinate (cap:mirror-surface): the other side's published surface mirrored as local nodes carrying which design, which hash, and when.
